metadata.note: Modern-day Metro-North Railroad network, as of the GTFS feed pulled from http://rrgtfsfeeds.s3.amazonaws.com/gtfsmnr.zip. Route geometry is taken from shapes.txt in that feed (real surveyed track alignment, simplified to a 40 m tolerance) -- an earlier version of this layer drew each route as straight hops between station coordinates, which wrongly showed the Hudson and Harlem lines diverging inside Manhattan; in reality they share the four-track Park Avenue main line out of Grand Central, through the Park Avenue Tunnel and over the Park Avenue Bridge, and split at Mott Haven Junction in the Bronx, while the New Haven Line stays with the Harlem Line until Woodlawn Junction. Frequency (headway_min, from real scheduled trip counts on a representative Wednesday), and avg_speed_kmh (from real scheduled trip duration) are all sourced directly from the agency's own GTFS feed, same methodology as data/amtrak.geojson. Each route is a single-year segment (2026) since GTFS has no historical depth. Historical segments (pre-2026) were added by estimating headway_min at researched ownership/frequency-milestone boundaries (predecessor-railroad origin dates, 1869/1872 corporate mergers, 1907-1914 electrification, Penn Central/Conrail era, Metro-North's Jan 1 1983 formation, etc., sourced from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites); unlike the GTFS-sourced 2026 segment, these older headway numbers are not derived from real historical timetables and should be read as illustrative estimates, not precise data.
not_yet_sourced: The Waterbury Branch has only a 7-point shape in the MTA feed, so that route alone is still close to a straight-line approximation; every other route follows real track geometry.

Only the 2026 segments carry measured service data (trip counts from the GTFS feed). Every historical headway_min in this layer is an estimate, and every avg_speed_kmh except the Metro-North features' is either an estimate or the modern GTFS figure reused for the Conrail era.

The New Haven's takeover of the Housatonic Railroad - and so of the Danbury Branch - is dated here only as 'soon after' the Housatonic's July 21 1887 lease of the Danbury and Norwalk; the exact year was not established.

Electrification dates (1907 to Croton-Harmon and North White Plains, 1907 Woodlawn-Stamford, 1914 to New Haven) are carried over from this layer's earlier research and were not re-checked against a primary source in this pass.

The 1837-1873 New York and Harlem feature draws the modern Grand Central alignment; the railroad's own Manhattan terminals of that era were further downtown and the Park Avenue approach was rebuilt repeatedly.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.ownership_audit: 2026-08-29: this layer used to draw every route in Metro-North green all the way back to 1837, so a map set to 1850 or 1900 showed a railroad that did not exist for another century. Each route is now split into one feature per operator, all sharing the route's single GTFS geometry, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4: Hudson River Railroad (1849-1869) then New York Central (1869-1968); New York and Harlem (1837-1873) then New York Central (1873-1968); New York and New Haven, merged 1872 into the New York, New Haven and Hartford (1849-1969); the Danbury and Norwalk (1852-1887), Naugatuck (1849-1887) and New Canaan (1868-1884) branch builders, each then passing to the New Haven; Conrail (1976-1983); and Metro-North itself (1983 onward). The Penn Central years - 1968 on the ex-New York Central lines, 1969 on the ex-New Haven ones, to 1976 - are deliberately NOT drawn here: data/penn_central.geojson already draws them on this same geometry, so the two layers form one continuous chain of operators. Four new colours were introduced for the predecessor companies (New York and Harlem #8AC926, Danbury and Norwalk #00B4D8, Naugatuck #FFCA3A, New Canaan #1982C4), each checked for separation against every colour already in data/; the Hudson River Railroad, New York Central, New Haven, Conrail and Metro-North colours were taken from features already in the repo so that each company keeps one colour map-wide.

segments.note: The Hudson River Railroad opened New York - Peekskill on September 29 1849 and reached Poughkeepsie by the end of that year. Its own Manhattan terminal was at Chambers Street, not Grand Central; the Park Avenue approach drawn here came later, with the New York Central. Cornelius Vanderbilt took control in 1864 and consolidated the Hudson River with the New York Central in 1869. estimated era boundary and frequency: no historical timetable was consulted, unlike the GTFS-sourced 2026 segment. Read headway_min as illustrative.

properties.line: New York and Harlem: New York – Chatham
properties.speed_source: Estimated, not measured: 1840s-60s steam service on the Harlem. The GTFS-derived figure on this route's Metro-North feature is the only measured speed in this layer.

segments.note: The New York and Harlem reached the village of Harlem on October 26 1837, White Plains on December 1 1844, Dover Plains on December 31 1848 and Chatham on January 19 1852. Its horsecars - the first street railway in the world, from 1832 - ran on the Manhattan streets south of the steam district, and the city barred steam south of 42nd Street from 1854; the line drawn here starts at 42nd Street and is steam-worked throughout, so the horsecar operation is context rather than anything this feature asserts. Vanderbilt bought the company in 1864 and the New York Central and Hudson River leased it on April 1 1873. estimated era boundary and frequency: no historical timetable was consulted, unlike the GTFS-sourced 2026 segment. Read headway_min as illustrative.
sources: Segment-level: the October 26 1837 arrival at Harlem, the December 1 1844 White Plains and December 31 1848 Dover Plains extensions, the January 19 1852 completion to Chatham, the 1854 steam ban south of 42nd Street, the 1864 Vanderbilt purchase and the April 1 1873 lease are all from the Wikipedia New York and Harlem Railroad article. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates.

segments.note: The Danbury and Norwalk Railroad opened its line from Norwalk north to Danbury on February 22 1852 and ran it independently for thirty-five years. The Housatonic Railroad leased it on July 21 1887, and the New York, New Haven and Hartford in turn leased the Housatonic soon after - so the New Haven came to this branch indirectly. estimated era boundary and frequency: no historical timetable was consulted, unlike the GTFS-sourced 2026 segment. Read headway_min as illustrative.
